newsitem.title: USA: To U.S. town, "UFO" means "Unite For Opportunity".
newsitem.headline: To U.S. town, "UFO" means "Unite For Opportunity".

text.p: The legend of an alien landing in the New Mexico desert draws eccentric UFO buffs into this conservative ranching town, but local residents are scrambling to welcome them -- and their dollars.

With tens of thousands of visitors expected in Roswell this week to celebrate the 50th anniversary of an alleged alien spacecraft crash just north of town, Roswell has embraced all things extraterrestrial in a bid to make a quick buck.

"Jeez, if you even drew an alien on a rock, you'd make some money this week," said Robbie Rogers, a barmaid at the Roswell Inn, whose hottest-selling cocktail is the "alien margarita," doctored with melon liqueur to turn it bright green.
All across this usually quiet town of 50,000 people, waving alien figures spring up from front yards, on motel signs and in stores.

T-shirts, jackets, cookies, pins, bottled water, baseball caps, flying disks and lollipops all carry pictures of skinny, light-skinned, four-fingered aliens with bulbous heads and huge eyes. Tourists line up to have their pictures taken alongside alien dummies and join bus tours to the alleged landing site.

Roswell's officials are delighted, saying it is high time the town took advantage of its position as the world's best-known site of a possible encounter with aliens. They expect between 60,000 and 100,000 people to visit this week.

"The market is huge," Mayor Thomas Jennings said on Tuesday at the International UFO Museum Research Centre, where UFO enthusiasts filled the gift shop and studied exhibits detailing "evidence" of the aliens' crash landing on July 4, 1947. "This is economic development."

Roswell grew up on the 19th-century cattle trade and was a major stop on the Goodnight-Loving Cattle Trail, which ran north into Colorado. The area's economy is now dominated by cattle, irrigation-based agriculture, and oil and gas.
Jennings said Roswell's average household income was about $20,000 and the UFO industry had provided a welcome economic boost in the 1990s.
Jeanette Miller, director of the Roswell Chamber of Commerce, said this week's events could pull in as much as $5 million. "It's an all-around plus," she said.

While Roswell's fame is based on the testimony of several of its residents, most people and the "witnesses" themselves draw a distinction between what is supposed to have happened here and the bizarre claims of some visitors due later this week, who tout theories that humans have been abducted and impregnated by extraterrestrials.

"You get a certain percentage of people who just want their name in the paper, who make it up to get attention," said Glenn Dennis, who claims he saw part of the UFO wreckage in 1947 and spoke to a military nurse who examined three dead aliens.
"I don't like all the hype and the commercialism," Dennis, who now runs the UFO museum, said.

The U.S. military flatly denies that a spacecraft landed here and that Air Force officials seized any alien corpses to conduct autopsies and tests, but the legend has grown rapidly in recent years, with Hollywood movies and television series focusing on the "Roswell Incident."
Most residents said they wished Roswell were famous for something other than aliens, but they take a live-and-let-live attitude to the town's wackier guests.

"We have some of our own crazies here in town, so a few more don't make much difference," said one saleswoman at the Cowtown Boot Company, across the street from the museum. "Besides, most of these people are regular folks. They're just interested in what happened, and it's only a few who are fanatical."
But there are some drawbacks to the town's fame. "I'm sick of truckers coming through here and asking me if I've seen a UFO," Corina Martinez, a downtown hardware store clerk, said.
